title: Newly diagnosed children
summary: A new T1D diagnosis involves learning practical skills while a child continues to grow, play and attend school.
why: Young children depend on adults to notice symptoms and coordinate care across settings.
how: Education is shared between the child, caregivers, school staff and paediatric diabetes team, with tasks matched to development.
example: A family asks the clinic to demonstrate one skill at a time and agrees on a school contact.
caution: Adult targets or meal routines may not suit a young child. Use a paediatric care plan.
question: Can a child participate without managing everything?
answer: Yes. Small age-appropriate tasks can build confidence with adult supervision.

title: Adolescence and puberty
summary: Puberty brings hormonal, physical and social changes that can affect glucose and self-care.
why: Changing insulin needs during growth can be mistaken for lack of effort.
how: Hormonal shifts can reduce insulin sensitivity, while sports, sleep and eating patterns may also change.
example: A teenager and parent choose which tasks can be independent and which still need shared support.
caution: Ask about distress, eating concerns and access to private clinical conversations.
question: Does a changing glucose pattern during puberty imply someone is doing something wrong?
answer: No. Growth and ordinary changes in routine are important context.

title: Young adult independence
summary: Moving out, starting college or changing clinics can shift responsibility for diabetes tasks quickly.
why: Medication access and follow-up can be interrupted during transitions.
how: A transition plan identifies who prescribes, how to obtain supplies and how to reach urgent advice.
example: Before moving cities a student arranges a first appointment, refill plan and local emergency contact.
caution: Do not wait until the last pen or sensor to identify a replacement source.
question: What belongs in a handover summary?
answer: Current treatment and devices, important recent results, emergency plans and clinic contacts.

title: Pregnancy planning and pregnancy
summary: Pregnancy planning includes discussing glucose goals, medicines and complication checks before conception where possible.
why: Glucose goals and insulin needs can differ before, during and after pregnancy.
how: Placental hormones, changing insulin sensitivity and delivery all influence needs. Specialist obstetric and diabetes care work together.
example: Someone planning a pregnancy asks for a medication review and advice on preconception care.
caution: Contact the team promptly with a positive pregnancy test. Do not stop insulin or change medicines independently.
question: Can I use the same CGM target band for every life stage?
answer: Pregnancy can use a different range and targets. Agree them with the specialist team.

title: Menstrual cycle and glucose
summary: Hormonal changes across the menstrual cycle can alter glucose patterns for some people.
why: Noticing a repeated pattern can reduce uncertainty and support a more informed clinical review.
how: Insulin sensitivity may vary across phases. Sleep, pain, appetite and activity may contribute as well.
example: A person compares several cycles privately before asking their team about recurring changes.
caution: A single high reading or one cycle does not establish a pattern. Unexpected symptoms still need assessment.
question: Does everyone become less sensitive at the same time?
answer: No. Direction and timing are individual.

title: Adult-onset type 1 diabetes
summary: Autoimmune type 1 diabetes can begin in adulthood, including in people initially thought to have type 2.
why: Correct classification affects insulin treatment, education and access to appropriate support.
how: Clinicians consider symptoms, course, antibodies and sometimes C-peptide rather than relying on age or weight alone.
example: An adult whose glucose rises despite initial tablets returns for reassessment.
caution: Rapid weight loss, vomiting or ketone symptoms require urgent care while classification is being investigated.
question: Does being an adult rule out T1D?
answer: No. Age alone cannot determine diabetes type.

title: Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA)
summary: LADA describes adult-onset autoimmune diabetes in which insulin production often declines more gradually.
why: Someone may initially manage without injected insulin and later need it as beta-cell function falls.
how: Antibodies can support an autoimmune cause. C-peptide helps assess remaining insulin production in clinical context.
example: An adult with an uncertain diagnosis asks why antibody and C-peptide tests answer different questions.
caution: Do not delay needed insulin while waiting for a label. Classification belongs with a clinician.
question: Does gradual onset mean the condition is harmless?
answer: No. Monitoring, treatment and education are still important.

title: Older adults with T1D
summary: Older adults with T1D have diverse abilities, support networks and health priorities.
why: Preventing severe lows and maintaining independence may change the balance of goals.
how: Vision, dexterity, memory, kidney function and medication burden can affect diabetes tasks.
example: Someone with reduced vision tries a device demonstration with their usual glasses and a supporter.
caution: Targets and technology should reflect function and preferences rather than age alone.
question: Does every older person need the same glucose goal?
answer: No. The care team should individualise it.

title: Aging with diabetes
summary: Aging with diabetes includes adapting care as health, roles and living circumstances change.
why: A plan that worked for many years can become harder after injury, illness or a move.
how: Periodic review can identify changes in device handling, meal patterns, circulation or support needs.
example: After a hand injury a person asks an educator to reassess their injection equipment.
caution: A change in ability calls for support and reassessment. Abruptly stopping background insulin is unsafe.
question: What can a family discuss before a move into supported living?
answer: Who is trained to give insulin, monitor glucose, recognise lows and obtain supplies.

title: Caregiver education
summary: Caregiver education prepares another person for specific tasks agreed with the person living with T1D.
why: A clear role reduces guesswork during a low or device problem.
how: Practical teaching includes recognising symptoms, locating supplies, following the written plan and practising when to call for help.
example: A grandparent rehearses a school-holiday handover with the family and diabetes educator.
caution: Use the person’s own plan. Do not give anything by mouth if they cannot swallow safely.
question: What should be written down?
answer: Contacts, the current plan, supply locations and clear instructions for urgent situations.
